children: By Natalie Andrews and Eliza Collins
STERLING HEIGHTS, Mich.-Vice President JD Vance had a message for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate here.

"Whatever you want to talk about, Abdul, keep my wife's name the hell out of your mouth because she's way out of your league," Vance said Monday at a political rally hosted by super PAC MAGA, Inc., where he boosted El-Sayed's Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

It was Vance's harshest and most direct attack yet on El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and who has previously brought up Second Lady Usha Vance, who is Hindu and the daughter of immigrants from India, in comments about the vice-president.

Earlier this month, Vance criticized El-Sayed's previous comments that efforts to ban Shariah law stemmed from white supremacy. Vance said he would love to go back in time to tell his grandfather, who he called Papaw. "That's not my Papaw's Democratic Party, my friends," he said.
El-Sayed then responded on X: "So do we think JD is taking Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no..."

The vice president said Monday he was especially sensitive to the comments because Usha Vance just gave birth to the couple's fourth child five weeks ago. The second lady did an interview with Fox News last weekend in which she said El-Sayed's comment made her laugh.

"Because yes, I never met JD's Mamaw and Papaw," Usha Vance told Fox News. "But I do know and love the children that they raised, his mom, his aunt and uncle. And they have never been anything but incredibly loving."
Vance on Monday accused El-Sayed of being divisive and having views that are "the root of this terrible evil, I believe, in the United States of America that is on the rise."

In a statement responding to Vance, El-Sayed said, "Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires. Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power."

Earlier Monday, El-Sayed criticized Vance during a press conference, noting the vice president attended Ohio State University, a longtime football rival to University of Michigan. He slammed the Trump administration's trade war with Canada and has said that for residents of Michigan-which shares a border with Canada-Canadians are much more popular than people from Ohio.

"I think Michigan is going to remind JD Vance why he should send his ass back to Ohio at the end of this day, at the end of November when we deliver a victory for Michiganders in this ridiculous trade war we have no business fighting," he said.
Before taking the stage, Vance met with the rabbi and security guards of Temple Israel, the synagogue in West Bloomfield Township, Mich., that was attacked in March, according to a spokesman.

Since winning the Michigan Democratic Senate primary, El-Sayed has had to address some of his more controversial statements. Last weekend, he apologized to the state's Jewish Democratic Caucus for comments he made after the synagogue attack, condemning it but connecting it to Israel's actions in the Middle East, saying "hurt people hurt people."

Vance was in Michigan campaigning for Rogers, the former congressman who is running against El-Sayed in one of the nation's most competitive Senate races. The seat is now held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. It is seen as Republicans' best chance to pick up a Senate seat in a year where President Trump's poll numbers are dragging down the party.

El-Sayed, a former public health official and progressive endorsed by Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders (I., Vt.) and others, has generated controversy within his own party. But Democratic leaders have rallied around his campaign since he narrowly won the primary earlier this month. Vance was also campaigning for Mike Bouchard, a Republican and Army veteran who is running in a competitive House seat north of Detroit against prosecutor Christina Hines, a Democrat.
